title: Security Sign-Off Is Coming For Chips — But Standards May Not Be Enough
gist: A closed-door DAC roundtable with Arteris, Cadence, Keysight EDA, Rambus, Siemens EDA, Synaptics and Synopsys concludes that a formal security sign-off step for chips is inevitable but that standards will not force it — the industry is diverging, not converging, as chiplets, custom AI silicon and proprietary interconnects proliferate. Rambus cites frontier models as cryptanalysis force multipliers (with 70% of HTTPS traffic on Cloudflare already using lattice-based post-quantum protocols, up from ~30% at the start of the year), while panelists argue weak implementations, not weak algorithms, are the real PQC exposure.

themes.theme: AI as a cryptanalysis force multiplier

insights.claim: Rambus' Scott Best cites a published result where a frontier-model tool running CryptanalysisBench was turned loose on the round-three candidate Hawk and on reduced-round AES, improved on known published attacks, and proved the resulting key strength was several hundred times smaller than believed.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: First concrete evidence that AI meaningfully shortens cryptanalysis timelines — raises the option value of crypto-agility in hardware and shortens the useful life of fixed-function crypto IP.
insights.quote: It improved the attacks that it knew about, that people have explored and published, and said, 'Well, we think it has this resulting key strength,' and the tool proved it was several hundred times smaller.
insights.locator: SE: Does the industry have a good understanding

insights.claim: Despite AI-assisted cryptanalysis, nothing currently suggests feasible, useful attacks against lattice cryptography, the basis of the major post-quantum standards now being deployed.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Calms the tail-risk case for a near-term PQC break; the investable exposure is in migration and implementation quality, not in the algorithms failing.
insights.quote: there's nothing out there right now that suggests that we have feasible, useful attacks against lattice cryptography, which is currently the basis of the major standards that are going into place
insights.locator: SE: Does the industry have a good understanding

insights.claim: The share of HTTPS traffic monitored by Cloudflare using the new lattice-based post-quantum protocols rose from around 30% at the start of the year to 70% now — a rate of protocol migration far faster than typical crypto transitions.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: PQC is already the default on the wire, so hardware that cannot accelerate lattice crypto is being stranded now, not in some future quantum era — a demand pull for PQC accelerator IP.
insights.quote: 70% of HTTPS traffic right now is using the new protocols... at the start of the year it was around 30%. It's now at 70%.
insights.locator: SE: Does the industry have a good understanding

insights.claim: Frontier models are explicitly framed as a force multiplier for both attackers and defenders, meaning the AI-security dynamic is symmetric rather than uniformly adversarial.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Argues against a simple 'AI breaks security' short thesis; the winners are firms that operationalize AI in verification and security analysis first.
insights.quote: But then, it's a force multiplier for both sides.
insights.locator: SE: Does the industry have a good understanding

insights.claim: Synopsys' Reed Hinkel argues the PQC exposure is not weak algorithms but weak implementations that leak information — once you start giving signatures to things, an attacker can work out the next attack vector.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Shifts the value from algorithm choice to implementation verification — good for security-analysis EDA tools and hardened crypto IP vendors, bad for roll-your-own crypto blocks.
insights.quote: it's not so much that the algorithm itself is weak, but that the implementations are weak. And if you have a weak implementation, that can actually leak information. It could be the camel's nose under the tent.
insights.locator: Hinkel: From some of the papers I've read

insights.claim: Synaptics' Mohit Arora notes PQC changes the ground rules well beyond the algorithm — runtime key generation and no key reuse impose an ongoing cost on the system profile, because security is only as good as the weakest link.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: PQC migration carries real silicon area, power and latency costs at the edge — a headwind for constrained IoT devices and a content opportunity for secure element vendors.
insights.quote: It's not just about the algorithm itself, but everything around it, because security is only as good as your weakest link.
insights.locator: Arora: Since it's all so new

themes.theme: Security sign-off becomes a design step

insights.claim: Arteris' Michal Siwinski states flatly that security sign-off is absolutely coming, echoed by Synopsys that eventually every design step will require a security sign-off just as it does functional sign-off.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A new mandatory sign-off step creates a durable new EDA revenue line — the same pattern that made timing, power and DFT sign-off tools structural businesses.
insights.quote: Security sign-off is absolutely coming.
insights.locator: Siwinski: Security sign-off is absolutely coming

insights.claim: The workable model for security sign-off is to treat security as another coverage asset within existing verification sign-off, because pragmatic solutions build on what teams already have rather than turning the design process on its head.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Predicts the winning product shape: security bolted into coverage-based verification flows, favoring incumbents with installed verification platforms over standalone security-tool startups.
insights.quote: You just consider security as another coverage kind of an asset of sorts, so at least you get that layer.
insights.locator: Siwinski: There are examples, but it's very fractured

insights.claim: Mandating compliance without extra budget or schedule relief is called out as the failure mode for security programs, implying adoption depends on making the added step cheap rather than on regulatory pressure.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Security tooling that adds meaningful cost or schedule will not be bought; low-friction integration is the commercial gating factor.
insights.quote: 'Hey, to comply with the project, you must now do A, B, C, and D. And no, you don't get more budget. And please be on schedule.'
insights.locator: Siwinski: There are examples, but it's very fractured

insights.claim: Security sign-off today is described as a fractured layer cake in which no uniform practice exists across the stack, and standards and regulations are not expected to force uniformity.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the assumption that regulation drives the security TAM — adoption will be customer-mandate-driven instead, so watch buyer requirements, not legislation.
insights.quote: Is there something uniform across the board? No, and I don't think the standards and regulations are going to force it, either.
insights.locator: SE: How soon? Shouldn't it have already happened?

insights.claim: A recurring practical prescription is that teams must simply start, because you cannot know what you do not know until you begin, and the discipline will be evolutionary rather than defined up front.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Signals a long, iterative adoption curve for hardware security tooling — revenue accretes gradually rather than through a step-change compliance deadline.
insights.quote: If you don't start, you'll never know what you don't know, and it will be evolutionary.
insights.locator: Siwinski: This is where I come back

insights.claim: Keysight's Alexander Petr raises the constraint that security sign-off assumes there are people in the stack capable of performing it — a skills gap that gates the whole model.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Talent scarcity favors automated and services-attached security offerings over tools that assume in-house expertise.
insights.quote: Assuming there are people in that stack who can do that.
insights.locator: Petr: Assuming there are people

themes.theme: Where the chip ends and the system begins

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Chris Giles identifies the boundary problem as the core ambiguity — you can have great chip security and terrible system security or vice versa, and with bad chip security a secure system is hopeless.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Explains why chip-level security certifications are necessary but not sufficient, and why system integrators, not chip vendors, will end up owning the liability.
insights.quote: You can have great chip security and terrible system security, or vice versa. So if you've got bad chip security, good luck with building a secure system.
insights.locator: Giles: I completely agree

insights.claim: The panel scopes 'hardware' security to include at least the lower firmware layer, on the reasoning that silicon without synchronized firmware is a useless piece of silicon.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Sets the practical scope of any hardware security sign-off product — it must span silicon plus low-level firmware, which is where the tool competition will be.
insights.quote: At least the firmware and better metal software have to be in sync. Otherwise, it's just a useless piece of silicon.
insights.locator: Siwinski: To be clear, when I say hardware

insights.claim: Synopsys' Hinkel identifies the critical missing link as the absence of a known-good formula from the bottom hardware layer up to meet system-level standards end to end, so IP vendors can honestly say they did their job while the problem remains unsolved.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: The gap between system-level standards and bottom-up implementation is the structural hole any winning security platform must fill — a defensible product opportunity.
insights.quote: The problem is that we don't have a known good formula from the bottom layer up to meet the standard end-to-end. That's really where the gap is.
insights.locator: Hinkel: This exposes a critical missing link

insights.claim: Closed systems such as Apple's are far easier to secure end to end, but the industry is moving toward open systems, so the easier case is receding rather than expanding.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Vertically integrated platform owners retain a structural security advantage over merchant-silicon ecosystems — a durable qualitative moat.
insights.quote: Going back to the Apple example, that system is extremely closed. Once you get to open systems, well, we're going the other way.
insights.locator: Giles: Yes, it's a much easier problem

insights.claim: Chiplets and heterogeneous disaggregation driven by reticle limits mean the industry is diverging rather than converging on security, directly undercutting the premise that standards will catch up.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Attack surface grows faster than standardization, so per-design security verification demand compounds — structurally bullish for security verification tooling and services.
insights.quote: With chiplets and heterogeneous disaggregation because of reticle limits, guess what? We're going the other way. We're not converging. We're diverging.
insights.locator: Siwinski: With chiplets and heterogeneous

insights.claim: Embedded systems containing FPGAs are singled out as making the chip-versus-system security boundary especially murky.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Reconfigurable logic in deployed systems is an under-priced security exposure in industrial and defense electronics.
insights.quote: As soon as you go into embedded systems with FPGAs, it's super murky.
insights.locator: Petr: As soon as you go into embedded systems

insights.claim: Microsoft has declared that equipment entering its data centers must be Caliptra-certified, requiring a large root of trust capable of firmware authentication and attestation and of signing attestation reports for all firmware in the system, with non-compliant equipment barred from installation.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A hyperscaler purchase mandate is a far stronger forcing function than any standards body — root-of-trust IP is becoming a condition of sale into the largest server buyers.
insights.quote: Microsoft has declared that if you're going to put equipment into our data center, it will be Caliptra-certified.
insights.locator: Best: Caliptra is an interesting approach

insights.claim: Rambus' Best flags the tension in Caliptra's governance — Microsoft owns the specification and permits zero deviation in hardware and software impacts while the code is entirely open source, which he suggests can produce universal bugs across all compliant equipment.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Monoculture risk: a mandated, zero-deviation, open root of trust concentrates systemic vulnerability across the entire data center fleet — a tail risk few price.
insights.quote: given they say there can be zero deviation allowed from the hardware and software impacts, and it's entirely open source, and now there are universal bugs?
insights.locator: Best: Caliptra is an interesting approach

insights.claim: Caliptra is described as continuity from the TCG/TPM lineage — the same people who spent years designing TPM working out how to put it on a chip — rather than a new invention, and as an implementation posing as a standard that we may see much more of.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: 'Reference implementation as de facto standard' is the emerging governance model in hardware security — track who controls the implementation, not who chairs the committee.
insights.quote: It's an interesting way of tying down what a foundation had, rather than just trusting. That's an interesting approach to do an implementation as a standard, basically, and we may see a lot more of that.
insights.locator: Best: It's an interesting way of tying down

insights.claim: Keysight's Petr argues that every operator of a big data center now builds its own TPUs, MPUs, GPUs, CPUs and integration layers — NVLink here, other things there — and these companies are not following standards because they have their own ideas, making standards a romantic notion.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Confirms the custom-silicon proliferation thesis from the tool-vendor side and implies security assurance must be per-customer bespoke — services-heavy, not product-scalable.
insights.quote: every single company comes up with their own TPUs, MPUs, GPUs, CPUs, and integration layers. It's NVLink here, other things there. It's like they're building up their own cities, literally, to feed the world's need for data centers.
insights.locator: What you're seeing right now is also how many companies

insights.claim: Analog designers entering historically all-digital domains such as HBM and PCI Express are generating multiple competing latency and speed improvement approaches, which multiplies standards rather than converging them.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Interface standards proliferation raises verification and interop test costs — a demand driver for signal-integrity and protocol test tooling.
insights.quote: now we're bringing analog concepts into something that was exclusively digital, and that leads to the problem of doing it one way or another. Now you have two standards, and a third guy comes along
insights.locator: SE: Does that mean more standards

insights.claim: Siemens' Giles concedes that even the ideal answer — a perfect set of standards — is unimplementable because no one knows how to enforce standards amid market pressures.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Enforcement, not authorship, is the binding constraint — invest behind mandates with commercial teeth (customer purchase conditions) rather than standards bodies.
insights.quote: obviously the answer is the perfect standard and the perfect set of standards. Except I don't know how you implement them and enforce them amid market pressures
insights.locator: Giles: This is ultimately why I said

insights.claim: Synopsys' Hinkel attributes Spectre and Meltdown to eagerness for cache performance — implementing caches directly from academic papers that had never undergone a security study of the architecture beforehand.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: A direct historical precedent for today's race to build unvetted custom AI accelerators — expect an analogous class of architectural vulnerability in bespoke datacenter silicon.
insights.quote: They were implementing caches directly from .edu papers. The problem was that those never had a security study of the architecture before they did it, and that's why Specter and Meltdown happened.
insights.locator: Hinkel: This also goes back to

insights.claim: The prescribed fix is to start with the security spec up front, as Arm did by bringing everything under one umbrella over time, rather than adding protections such as protected memory long after speculative execution shipped.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Architecture licensors that build security into the spec accrue trust advantage over ad hoc custom cores — a qualitative moat for Arm-style IP in security-sensitive markets.
insights.quote: They added protected memory long after they implemented speculative stuff.
insights.locator: Best: They added protected memory

insights.claim: Synaptics' Arora warns that over-specifying implementation detail is a double-edged sword, because when a specification goes down into the weeds on the implementation side, the specification itself becomes the attack surface.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Cuts against the 'more prescriptive standards' reflex — prescriptive specs create predictable, uniformly exploitable implementations, echoing the Caliptra monoculture concern.
insights.quote: When the specification goes down through the weeds on the implementation side, that becomes the actor itself.
insights.locator: Arora: It's a double-edged sword

insights.claim: Petr notes that the shift from copper to fiber optics for most wired communication removes electromagnetic emission and injection paths but opens different attack layers that may not have been thought through.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: Optical interconnect adoption in data centers changes rather than eliminates the physical attack surface — a new and largely unexamined security category.
insights.quote: copper emits fields, so it can potentially inject something there. Wired fiber doesn't have that problem. So, are there different layers you can attack now?
insights.locator: Petr: IoT is mostly mobile devices

insights.claim: Adding neural networks into wireless transmitter-receiver chains to dynamically adapt the communication layer is stacking new complexity onto stacks already vulnerable because of open-source code, with security assumed rather than designed.
insights.speaker: Ann Mutschler
insights.so_what: AI-native radio is arriving before anyone has secured it — a forward risk for IoT and edge device makers and an opening for supply-chain visibility tooling.
insights.quote: It goes back to, 'Do you have visibility? Can you track it? And are you monitoring?'
insights.locator: Petr: IoT is mostly mobile devices
